newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Amoco sees $10 bln in chemicals sales.
newsitem.headline: Amoco sees $10 bln in chemicals sales.

text.p: U.S.-based petroleum group Amoco Corp said on Monday it expected sales from its chemicals business to more than double over the next four years to $10 billion, much of it from rapidly-growing Asian markets.

"Our objective for our chemicals portfolio is to achieve $10 billion in profitable sales over four years. That is our current objective," said Enrique Sosa, executive vice president for Amoco's chemicals sector.
The chemicals business currently generates about $4 billion of the Amoco group's total annual sales of $31 billion.

Sosa was to open Amoco's 1.2 billion ringgit ($480 million) purified terephthalic acid (PTA) plant in Malaysia's east coast town of Kuantan on Tuesday. PTA is used in the manufacturing of polyester and other textiles.
The plant, 100 percent owned by Amoco, has the capacity to produce 500,000 tonnes. Amoco says it is Asia's largest single unit PTA plant.
"We believe it is very important for us to be in Asia and this is where the big part of the polyester market growth is going to take place," Sosa said.
Polyesters are used to make clothes, soft drink bottles, food packaging, magnetic recording tape and tyre reinforcement, among other things. Malaysia has imported PTA up until now.
Sosa acknowledged it was not the best time to open a PTA plant with supply expected to outstrip demand in the near future.
"There's no question that in 1997 and 1998 there will be somewhat of an oversupply," Sosa said.

The company has decided to end the construction of a petrochemicals plant in Decatur, Illinois and has cancelled plans to build a paraxylene plant in Paris under a joint venture with Total Sa Paraxylene is the feedstock for PTA.
But the PTA industry in Asia over the long-term was a "sound investment", Sosa said.
"The fundamentals of PTA in Asia are very sound," he said. "We're staying the course here."
Asia should see growth of eight to nine percent in PTA demand, he said. "We use that kind of growth rate to plan our investments."
But the future over-capacity in the industry depends on the growth plans of Korean PTA producers, he said.
PTA prices, however, should recover in the short term after being depressed for nearly a year as the polyester industry replenishes depleted stocks, Sosa said.
"We foresee an increase in PTA prices by the fourth quarter of 1996," he said. "The de-stocking that took place over the last six to nine months is behind us."

Amoco's Malaysian plant began commercial production in June and is currently operating at 75 percent capacity. Half of the production will be exported initially, mostly to Southeast Asian countries. But eventually the company expects to sell 80 percent of its output to Malaysian customers, Sosa said.

Feedstock for the plant will come from Amoco's joint venture paraxylene plant in Singapore, in which Exxon Corp has a 50 percent stake, Amoco 45 percent and Taiwan's CAPCO -- a joint venture between Amoco and the China Petroleum Corp -- has five percent.
